title: 'Deeply missed'; Toronto officer, 2 others honoured year after their murders
article: When Const. Andrew Hong headed out to pick up a coffee and a sandwich on his lunch break, it should have been as routine as routine can be.
But there is nothing routine about policing - not anymore.
In the past year or so, there have been 11 police funerals for brave officers who died in the line of duty.

One year ago, the beloved Toronto officer nicknamed Honger rode his motorcycle over to a Tim Hortons. He was on his break from teaching other officers from many services about motorbikes - something Hong was an expert in.

He even drove over on his police bike. How could Hong ever know there would be a killer there just waiting for him to do that? Just as we mark the anniversary of one horrific, senseless slaughter comes the reminder of another that hurts just as much. While the memory from the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks on the Twin Towers in New York lingers, the pain of what happened Sept. 12, 2022, also stings.

Hong was gutlessly stalked, ambushed and shot dead in a Mississauga Tim Hortons, and those wounds are still raw. Seconds after the 48-year-old motorcycle cop fell to the floor - hit by a bullet in a sneak attack - his killer embarked upon a bloody rampage that would also see the slaying of 38-year-old Milton auto shop owner Shakeel Ashraf, international student Satwinder Singh, 28, and the wounding of two others.

The killer, Sean Petrie, 40, was fatally shot by police officers in Const. Andrew Hong was a "hero to all of us," his daughter Mia says. FAMILY PHOTO a Hamilton cemetery. Nobody is missing that guy. He had been in and out of the court system for years. Good riddance.
Nothing can bring back his victims. Nothing anybody can say will fix this. But the slain will be remembered at a memorial event on Tuesday.
While Hong's peers remain sad, they are still angry, too.

"Sadly, it doesn't seem like much has changed," Toronto Police Association president Jon Reid said. "Our members are still being deliberately injured on duty and we are still seeing repeat violent offenders released into the community."

While seeing "little effort from the federal government to make any of the changes," Reid said, "we will not stop asking for these changes and we will not stop demanding respect for our members and law-abiding citizens."
Reid called Hong a "larger-than-life personality" who's "deeply missed by his colleagues and family."

When Hong was slain, his brothers and sisters at Toronto Police Traffic Services displayed his motorcycle and helmet and told stories of this popular figure, a gentle giant known on the streets for his famous smile. They will be on display again Tuesday.

"I am so proud of everything you have done and so proud to call you dad," his daughter Mia wrote in a tribute to him. "You came to every sports game and even woke up early and took a three-hour train to catch my last basketball game of the tournament."
She said Hong was the best dad, husband and son.
"I am so sorry this happened to you," Mia wrote. "You were truly a hero to all of us and will always be remembered that way."

Chief Myron Demkiw has invited Mia, Hong's wife Jenny and son Alex to traffic services for a special remembrance event. "Const. Hong had a reputation for being kind and generous, and he loved being a member of the motor squad, where he served as a motorcycle officer for 14 years," Demkiw said in a prepared statement on Monday.
A year later, the biggest question that remains is why.
What we do know is Petrie had been a career criminal, was living out of his car, was using a nearby gym to shower and once worked at Ashraf's shop but left acrimoniously.
We don't know why he targeted Hong.

We do know he waited 15 minutes in front of that Tim Hortons and entered once Hong was inside and made eye contact before going into the bathroom, from which he exited firing a gun. After an unsuccessful attempt to get Hong's police handgun, Petrie fled before shooting and wounding someone else to take his car.
A year later, Peel Regional Police are still investigating. But on this Sept. 12, the focus is not on how Hong, Ashraf and Singh died, but on how they lived.
